full_judgment:
6. Mr. Gour Gopal Saha, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner, submits that the learned Subordinate Judge evidently erred in law in misappreciating the scope of the provisions of section 95A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and the same has resulted in an error in his decision occasioning failure of justice. He next submitted that on the assertion of the plaintiff himself that he paid a further sum of Taka 6000.00 to the defendant for the suit land which was earlier sold to the plaintiff, it is evident that the Kabala in question dated 26th Falgun, 1379 BS was patently a deed of usufructuary mortgage and, as such, was liable to be redeemed under section 95A of the SAT Act and the Sub-Divisional Magistrate was the final authority for ordering redemption of the suit property and, as such, the present suit was not maintainable and the court of appeal below erred in law in passing the impugned order without considering this admitted position of the case and the same has occasioned the failure of justice. He also submitted that the petitioner obtained possession in the said land in due course of law after getting the order of redemption dated 15.11.83 passed by the Sub-Divisional Magistrate, Jamalpur and since then has been in possession thereof. He next submitted that it is evident that the court of appeal below erred in law in not holding that the present suit for simple declaration without a prayer for recovery of khas possession on payment of ad valorem court fee is not maintainable in law. He further submitted that under provisions of section 44 of the Evidence Act, any party to a suit or other proceeding may show that any judgment, order or decree which is relevant under sections 40, 41 and 42 and which has been proved by the adverse party, was delivered by a court not competent to deliver it, or was obtained by fraud or collusion. He also submitted that the order of redemption dated 15.11.83 passed by the learned Sub-Divisional Magistrate, Jamalpur in Miscellaneous Petition No. 23 can only be challenged by the plaintiff-opposite party who contested the same by filing written objection and unsuccessfully brought an appeal before the learned District Judge, Jamalpur, only on the ground of want of jurisdiction of the court or on the ground of fraud or collusion. He lastly, submitted that under Order XIV rule 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure where issues both of law and fact arise in the same suit, and the court is of the opinion that the case or any part thereof may be disposed of on the issues of law only, it shall try those issues first, and for that purpose may, if it thinks fit, postpone the settlement of the issues of fact until after the issues of law have been determined. 

 16. Mr Saha next placed the case of Rakhal Chandra Das and others vs. Benecha Khatun and others, reported in 24 DLR 42. He argued that the learned court of appeal below did not consider that the defendant-petitioner had already taken delivery of possession through court on 8.4.85 and, as such, the suit in its present form without a prayer for khas possession is not maintainable. In the case reported in 24 DLR 42 it was held that the writ of delivery of possession, even if taken to be symbolical delivery of possession, has, in the eye of law, the effect of actual possession so far as judgment debtors are concerned. In the instant case the order of redemption dated 15.11.83 was passed on contest against the plaintiff-opposite party and thereafter delivery of possession was taken through court and, as such, there is substance in the submission of Mr. Saha that the suit is not maintainable without a prayer for khas possession. 

 17. It may be further stated here that section 42 of the Specific Relief Act also is a bar against the plaintiff-opposite party in getting a decree for simple declaration as the plaintiff being able to seek further relief by way of recovery of khas possession has failed to do so.
